questions.q: How does the Vantage Utilities case study's integration direction differ from Lessons 1-3?
options: It is identical in direction -- Salesforce still initiates every call
An external application that Vantage doesn't fully control calls in to Salesforce on behalf of individual end customers, reversing the direction of the earlier case studies
Vantage Utilities does not use Salesforce at all
The portal only ever reads data and can never create any Salesforce record
questions.explain: Lessons 1-3 all involve Salesforce calling out or another system pushing into Salesforce under Vantage's own control end to end. Here, an external, separately-deployed portal calls in to Salesforce on behalf of specific customers, which is a genuine reversal that changes which design questions matter most.

questions.q: This lesson distinguishes authentication from authorization. Which statement correctly describes the difference?
options: They are the same question asked twice, so only one check is actually needed
Authentication verifies who or what is making the call; authorization determines what that specific caller is allowed to do, scoped to a specific end user
Authorization happens before authentication in every design
Authentication only applies to human users, never to applications
questions.explain: Authentication answers "who is calling," while authorization answers "what is this caller allowed to do, for which end user." A system can be authenticated correctly and still be catastrophically over-permissioned if authorization isn't separately scoped per customer.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the most common real-world cause rate limiting actually protects against?
options: Only deliberate, malicious attackers attempting to overwhelm the org
A bug in the calling application's own code, such as a retry loop that doesn't back off, generating far more traffic than any real customer would
Salesforce's own servers randomly generating excess traffic
Rate limiting has no practical use case and is purely a theoretical concern
questions.explain: The lesson specifically notes that rate limiting most often saves an org from its own well-intentioned but buggy client code -- like an unbounded retry loop or a page re-fetching on every keystroke -- not just from malicious attackers.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say API versioning matters for the Vantage portal integration specifically?
options: Because the portal and Salesforce's API surface won't change on the same schedule, and an unversioned endpoint change would break the portal with no warning
Because Salesforce requires every integration to use exactly one API version forever
Because versioning eliminates the need for any authentication
Because the portal is hosted inside Salesforce and shares its deploy schedule
questions.explain: Versioning lets two teams that don't deploy in lockstep keep working against the same integration: existing callers keep working unchanged on an old version while the portal team upgrades to a new version on its own schedule, instead of being broken by a surprise change.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say Lesson 8's security review will spend disproportionate time on this particular case study?
options: Because the caller is external and acts on behalf of individual customers, so the review has to scrutinize exactly how customer-level authorization is enforced, not just assumed
Because this is the only case study that uses any authentication at all
Because Vantage Utilities has no Service Cloud license
Because external integrations never need a security review in practice
questions.explain: Because this integration lets an external, less-trusted caller act on behalf of specific end customers, the security review has extra weight here -- it needs to verify customer-level authorization is genuinely enforced, consider stolen-session scenarios, and confirm suspicious access is logged and detectable.
